# How to Use Claude for Multi-Step Daily Tasks

Imagine having a patient colleague who can sit with you through your whole to-do list — drafting emails, sorting priorities, researching a decision, even writing a basic spreadsheet formula — all in one uninterrupted conversation. That's what using Claude for multi-step tasks feels like. Unlike a simple search engine, Claude remembers what you've already told it and builds on that as you go.

This guide walks you through exactly how to set up your account, start your first task, and get results you can actually use. You don't need any technical background — just a web browser and about ten minutes.

## What you'll need before you start

- A free account at **claude.ai** (you can sign up with an email address, or using your Google or Apple account)
- The free plan is fine to start — there's no obligation to upgrade
- A device with a web browser (desktop or mobile)

## Step 1 — Create your account and sign in

Open your browser and go to **claude.ai**. You'll land on a page with a "Sign up" option. Click it.

You'll be asked to choose how to register. The quickest way is to connect an existing Google or Apple account — the page will redirect you to confirm, then bring you straight into the app. Alternatively, enter your email address and create a password. Either way, check your inbox for a verification email if one arrives.

**What you'll see after signing in:** The main chat screen. There's a wide text box near the bottom of the page where you type your messages, and a sidebar on the left showing your past conversations (it will be empty on first login).

💬 **Example:** If you prefer email signup, just enter something like `yourname@email.com` and follow the prompts to set a password.

**You'll know it worked when** the chat input box is visible and ready — you can click inside it and start typing immediately.

---

## Step 2 — Start a new conversation

Look at the left sidebar. You should see either a button labelled **"New Chat"** or a similar option (the exact wording may change slightly as the interface updates — look for anything that creates a fresh conversation).

Click it. The main area will clear, showing only the input box.

**What you'll see after clicking:** A clean chat window. There might be a small greeting message from Claude, but otherwise the screen is empty and ready for your first message.

💬 **Example prompt you can copy:**
> "Hi Claude, I want to work through three things with you today: sort my task list, draft two emails, and research a local tradie. Is that okay?"

**You'll know it worked when** the sidebar shows a new conversation entry (usually with today's date or "New Chat"), confirming your session has started.

---

## Step 3 — Give Claude a clear, single task first

Before dumping everything at once, start with one specific job. Click inside the text input box at the bottom of the screen and type your request. Be concrete about what you want Claude to produce.

**What you'll see after sending:** Claude's response will appear in the chat, styled as a written reply. It will build on your request step by step. You'll then see the input box is still there below the reply — you can keep talking.

💬 **Example prompt you can copy:**
> "I've pasted below a list of my emails. Can you sort them into three groups: needs a reply today, can wait until later this week, and can be ignored? After that, draft a polite reply to the urgent one."

*(After sending that message, paste your email list directly into the chat — Claude can read it and work with it.)*

**You'll know it worked when** Claude's reply addresses your specific request. If you asked for a list, you'll see a list. If you asked for a draft email, you'll see draft text ready to read.

---

## Step 4 — Ask for the next step in the same conversation

Once Claude has finished your first task, move to the next one without starting a new conversation. Just type your next request in the same chat.

**What you'll see:** Claude will respond to the new request, referencing your earlier messages if relevant. The conversation grows, with each message visible above.

💬 **Example prompt you can copy:**
> "Great, thanks. Now can you help me draft two emails? The first is to James to push back our meeting to Thursday — he suggested Wednesday at 3pm but I'm not available. Keep it brief and friendly. The second is a thank-you note to my sister after she helped me move house last weekend."

**You'll know it worked when** Claude produces two separate draft emails, clearly labelled, that you can read through and edit before using.

---

## Step 5 — Ask for a summary or action list at the end

When you've worked through all your tasks, ask Claude to pull everything together. This gives you a clean record you can copy and paste elsewhere.

**What you'll see:** Claude will compile a summary — it might list the drafts it wrote, decisions it helped you make, or steps it outlined for something you're working on.

💬 **Example prompt you can copy:**
> "Can you summarise everything we've covered in this conversation? List the two email drafts, the task prioritisation we did, and the three tradie options I asked about."

**You'll know it worked when** you see a clearly formatted summary covering all the work you completed together. You can now copy it to your notes, calendar, or email.

---

## Common mistakes

### Mistake 1: Asking for too much at once
**What happens:** You paste a huge brief — "organise my whole week, write my business plan, and plan my holiday" — and get shallow, generic answers.  
**Fix:** Break it into separate conversations or work through one thing at a time within one session. "Let's do one thing at a time — first, my week. Then we'll move on."

### Mistake 2: Vague requests that give vague answers
**What happens:** You write "help me with my emails" and get general advice instead of actual sorting or draft replies.  
**Fix:** Name exactly what you want produced. "Sort these five emails into priority order and draft a reply to the most urgent one" is much more useful than a vague request.

### Mistake 3: Forgetting to review before using
**What happens:** You copy and paste a drafted email to a client without reading it, and realise Claude used the wrong name or suggested a meeting time you can't actually offer.  
**Fix:** Always read through the output before using it. Think of Claude as a first-draft writer — you're the editor who checks it before it goes out.

---

## What this means for you

- **If you want to save time at home:** Use Claude to draft tricky messages — to a landlord, a school, a service provider. Describe the situation in plain English and ask for a polite but firm email you can send yourself.

- **If you run a small business or work in a team:** Claude is useful for the jobs you keep putting off. Draft a standard supplier inquiry, summarise meeting notes, or work through a decision by asking for pros and cons.

- **If you're new to AI:** Start with one small, real task you have today — something like drafting a reply or summarising an article. Get comfortable with how the conversation works before trying anything complex.

Claude won't replace the thinking you do — but it can handle the first draft of many everyday tasks, giving you back time for the work that actually needs you.
